prompt: Russian literature as a major world tradition essentially begins with which writer?
explanation: Russian literature is surprisingly young. While Western Europe had Dante by 1320 and Shakespeare by 1600, Russian literature in any modern sense begins around 1820. In two short decades Pushkin created the foundation; every subsequent Russian writer looks back to him. He died in a duel at 37.

prompt: Pushkin's most influential work, told in 389 stanzas of an invented 14-line form, is:
explanation: Eugene Onegin (1825-1832) is a novel in verse. Tatyana — serious, deeply read, morally clear, capable of sacrifice — became the prototype of the Russian heroine. Pushkin's Russian was the language Russian literature was written in afterward. He took a culture borrowing heavily from French and made it Russian.

prompt: The recurring Russian literary type — aristocratic, talented, with no useful place in society — embodied by Lermontov's Pechorin and Goncharov's Oblomov is the _________ man.
explanation: Lermontov's A Hero of Our Time (1840) is sometimes called the first Russian psychological novel. Pechorin — bored, intelligent, destructive of others and himself — became the archetype. The 'superfluous man' makes a kind of national diagnosis recurring through 19th-century Russian fiction.

prompt: What's a defining feature of the Russian literary tradition Pushkin established?
options: Moral seriousness — literature as a way of asking how to live, including the 'cursed questions' (what to do, who is to blame, what is to be done, does God exist)
correctAnswer: Moral seriousness — literature as a way of asking how to live, including the 'cursed questions' (what to do, who is to blame, what is to be done, does God exist)
explanation: Russian writers, working in a society without free political speech, took on tasks that Western philosophers and journalists handled elsewhere. The author as moral figure — a quasi-prophetic status — has been a recurring feature. Tolstoy's pronouncements on war and peace, Solzhenitsyn's exposure of the Gulag — readers expected literature to do moral work.

prompt: Match each early Russian writer to a contribution:

pairs.right: Eugene Onegin; foundation of modern Russian literature; died in duel at 37
A Hero of Our Time; first Russian psychological novel; died in duel at 26
Established that Russian literature would be unusually serious — fusing entertainment with moral inquiry

explanation: Pushkin and Lermontov together established Russian literature's distinctive seriousness. Where French and English writers often kept literary entertainment and moral inquiry separate, Russian writers tended to fuse them. Both also died young in duels — a Romantic-era pattern reinforcing the literary mythology.

prompt: Which Gogol short story did Dostoevsky reportedly say 'we all came out of'?
explanation: 'The Overcoat' (1842) became one of the most influential short stories in world literature. Akaky Akakievich, a humble copying clerk, saves to buy a coat; thugs steal it; the bureaucracy refuses to help; he dies of distress; his ghost haunts Petersburg. The story finds moral depth in figures the official society dismissed.

prompt: What is Gogol's Dead Souls (1842) about?
options: Chichikov, a sketchy bureaucrat, traveling through provincial Russia buying 'dead souls' — serfs who have died but remain on tax rolls — to use as collateral for a loan
correctAnswer: Chichikov, a sketchy bureaucrat, traveling through provincial Russia buying 'dead souls' — serfs who have died but remain on tax rolls — to use as collateral for a loan
explanation: Dead Souls's premise is dark comedy. The book is a tour of Russian provincial types — landowners ranging from the dreamy Manilov to the miserly Plyushkin — each grotesquely vivid. Gogol intended a Russian Divine Comedy in three parts. He completed Part 1, burned a draft of Part 2, fell into religious mania, and died at 42.

prompt: Gogol's most successful play, in which a small provincial town mistakes a penniless Petersburg clerk for a government inspector, is The _________ General.
explanation: The play (1836) is a masterpiece of provincial satire. Every official is venal in a different way. Tsar Nicholas I supported the play, reportedly remarking 'Everyone got what they deserved, and I most of all.' Whether the comment is true, the play was politically ambiguous in a way that protected its author.

prompt: What's Gogol's most influential mode for later world literature?
options: Surrealism in realist surfaces — strange events in matter-of-fact prose; runs from Gogol through Kafka through García Márquez
correctAnswer: Surrealism in realist surfaces — strange events in matter-of-fact prose; runs from Gogol through Kafka through García Márquez
explanation: A nose detaches from a face and walks the streets in uniform. The story is told as if it's news. This mode runs from Gogol through Kafka through García Márquez through contemporary writers. Reading Gogol — particularly the Petersburg stories — is part of how literature got modern.

prompt: Match each Gogol contribution to its description:

pairs.right: Akaky Akakievich as prototype of literature taking the obscure seriously
Mayor and officials of The Inspector General as recurring national type
Lyrical, slangy, pseudo-bureaucratic, absurd within paragraphs

explanation: Nabokov said Gogol's sentences 'lurch and twitch like a great writer who hasn't learned how to write.' His combination of grotesque physicality, surreal events told straight, and shifting tones produces effects no other Russian writer matches.

prompt: Tolstoy's two greatest novels are War and Peace (1867) and:
explanation: After a religious crisis in his fifties, Tolstoy renounced his earlier work and produced moral and religious writing — plus a few late masterpieces (The Death of Ivan Ilyich, The Kreutzer Sonata, Hadji Murat). He became a global moral figure; Gandhi corresponded with him. He died at 82 trying to leave home.

prompt: Anna Karenina opens with which famous line?
options: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'
'All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way'
'In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit'
correctAnswer: 'All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way'
explanation: The novel runs two parallel plots: Anna's adulterous affair with Vronsky and its destruction; Levin (an autobiographical figure) marrying Kitty and finding provisional peace. Each plot illuminates the other. Tolstoy refuses to judge Anna — the moral position is more complicated than the epigraph 'Vengeance is mine; I will repay' suggests.

prompt: Viktor Shklovsky's term for Tolstoy's habit of describing familiar things as if for the first time is _________.
explanation: A character watching an opera sees absurd, painted people on a wooden platform making strange noises. The familiar is made strange so we see it. Combined with total access to character minds and moral clarity through detail, defamiliarisation is one of the techniques that makes Tolstoy's world feel indistinguishable from the actual one.

prompt: What's Tolstoy's argument about historical causation in War and Peace?
options: Great-man theories are wrong — history is the cumulative effect of millions of small decisions, not the will of generals or emperors
correctAnswer: Great-man theories are wrong — history is the cumulative effect of millions of small decisions, not the will of generals or emperors
explanation: Tolstoy argues at length, sometimes tediously, against great-man theories. The book interleaves novelistic narrative with historical essay. What makes the book unbeatable is the texture of consciousness — Andrei wounded staring at the sky, Natasha at her first ball, Pierre witnessing a French execution.

prompt: Match each Tolstoy late work to a description:

pairs.right: A high-court judge's slow death and his recognition that his entire life was wrong
A wealthy merchant and his servant lost in a snowstorm
Caucasian rebel betrayed by Russian forces; often called Tolstoy's most perfect short novel

explanation: The late work is austere and morally focused. Some readers prefer it to the panoramic earlier books. Tolstoy's What Is Art? (1898) argued that most art was elite distraction; real art should communicate moral feeling to ordinary people. Most of the canonical works he had loved — including his own great novels — failed this test.

prompt: Dostoevsky was sentenced to death in 1849, given a last-minute reprieve at the firing squad, and spent how many years in a Siberian penal colony?
options: Four years (then four more in the army)
correctAnswer: Four years (then four more in the army)
explanation: The mock execution had been deliberate state theater. Dostoevsky returned to Petersburg in 1859 debt-ridden, an epileptic, eventually addicted to gambling. The major novels were written in the last 15 years of his life: Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot (1869), Demons (1872), The Brothers Karamazov (1880).

prompt: What does Crime and Punishment (1866) ultimately argue about Raskolnikov's theory that 'extraordinary' people have the right to kill?
options: Ideas have consequences; theoretical justifications cannot survive contact with what murder actually feels like
correctAnswer: Ideas have consequences; theoretical justifications cannot survive contact with what murder actually feels like
explanation: The theory was pure thought; the act produces a self that cannot bear what it has done. The novel's technique — feverish, claustrophobic, urgent — depicts Raskolnikov's guilt and paranoia, with the saintly Sonya pushing him toward eventual confession. The detective Porfiry circles him in long psychological cat-and-mouse interrogations.

prompt: Mikhail Bakhtin's term for Dostoevsky's distinctive technique — multiple competing voices, none ultimately framed by a single authoritative narrator — is _________.
explanation: Most novelists, including Tolstoy, have an authoritative narrator above the characters. In Dostoevsky, characters speak with voices the author doesn't fully contain. Ivan Karamazov makes the case against God so well that critics still debate whether Dostoevsky succeeds in answering him. The novels accommodate readers across politics — they argue with themselves.

prompt: What is 'The Grand Inquisitor' in The Brothers Karamazov?
options: A parable Ivan tells Alyosha — Christ returns to 16th-century Seville and is arrested by the Inquisition, who explains why the Church rejected Christ's gift of freedom
A villain in the murder mystery
A monk at Father Zosima's monastery
correctAnswer: A parable Ivan tells Alyosha — Christ returns to 16th-century Seville and is arrested by the Inquisition, who explains why the Church rejected Christ's gift of freedom
explanation: The Grand Inquisitor explains: humans cannot bear freedom; they want bread, mystery, authority. Christ kisses the Inquisitor and leaves. Combined with Ivan's 'rebellion' (he 'returns the ticket' to a heaven where children suffer) and Father Zosima's teaching ('love everyone, even the bad'), it makes The Brothers Karamazov perhaps the most morally serious novel in any language.

prompt: Match each Dostoevsky text to a description:

pairs.right: Often called the first existential novel; rejects rational utopianism in favor of free will, even when destructive
Raskolnikov tests his 'extraordinary man' theory by murder; cannot survive its consequences
Three legitimate sons, an illegitimate one, a murdered father; vast philosophical investigation

explanation: Existentialists in the 20th century — Sartre, Camus — drew on Notes from Underground directly. The Underground Man as anti-hero, isolated, conscious to the point of paralysis, became a recognisable type running through Hamsun's Hunger and Sartre's Nausea into much of postmodern fiction.

prompt: Anton Chekhov was, in addition to being a writer, a:
options: Doctor by training, who ran his medical practice for much of his life and treated peasants for free
correctAnswer: Doctor by training, who ran his medical practice for much of his life and treated peasants for free
explanation: Chekhov is, in some ways, the antithesis of Dostoevsky and Tolstoy. He wrote no vast novels — he wrote short stories and four major plays. He didn't argue with God, didn't write moral tracts, didn't preach. His method is restraint. He died at 44 of tuberculosis.

prompt: Chekhov's four major plays are The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and:
explanation: All four plays end with their characters in much the situation they started, only diminished. The 'action' is mostly internal — small recognitions, slow defeats. The premiere of The Seagull failed in Petersburg; Stanislavski's reproduction at the Moscow Art Theater the next year was a sensation. The plays needed a new style of acting.

prompt: Chekhov's plays invented modern dramatic _________ — a character's surface words rarely matching what they're really feeling.
explanation: A daughter refuses tea; the audience understands she is grieving. A man talks about the weather; he is in love. A long pause holds more meaning than the speech that interrupted it. Stanislavski developed his acting system partly to enable actors to play subtext. Pinter, Mamet, Sondheim, naturalist film acting — all rely on it.

prompt: Which Chekhov story did the author himself name as his favorite?
explanation: In 'The Student' (1894), a young divinity student tells two old peasant women about Peter's denial of Christ. The story they share unites generations across centuries. Other masterpieces include 'The Lady with the Dog' (1899) and 'The Bishop' (1902). Chekhov demonstrated that a short story doesn't need conventional plot — it needs precise observation and the right detail.

prompt: Match each Chekhov contribution to a description:

pairs.right: Sees characters' weaknesses without contempt and strengths without inflation
Characters mostly fail to become what they wanted to be; doesn't condemn — shows the human situation

pairs.left: Influence on the modern short story
pairs.right: Mansfield, Joyce, Hemingway, Carver, Munro — most short fiction since 1900 is in his shadow

explanation: Reading Chekhov teaches a skill more than a subject: to see ordinary people and ordinary moments without distortion or evasion. Many writers have tried; few do it as well. His effect builds slowly — many readers don't fully understand a Chekhov story until they reread it.

prompt: What did the Soviet state demand of writers after 1917?
options: Socialist realism — heroic depictions of workers, peasants, and Party
correctAnswer: Socialist realism — heroic depictions of workers, peasants, and Party
explanation: Writers who couldn't or wouldn't comply faced exile, imprisonment, or execution. Despite this — sometimes because of it — Soviet-era Russian literature produced some of its greatest writers. They wrote in code, in private, in exile, or after long delays.

prompt: Whose long-suppressed satirical-theological masterpiece The Master and Margarita features the Devil arriving in Stalin's Moscow with a giant talking cat named Behemoth?
explanation: Bulgakov's masterpiece, written in the 1930s, was published only in 1966-67 (censored) and fully in 1973. The novel juxtaposes a slapstick Moscow plot with a sober retelling of Pontius Pilate's trial of Christ. The cat Behemoth became a cultural figure; the book became one of the most beloved in Russian literature.

prompt: Solzhenitsyn's three-volume documentary history of the Soviet prison-camp system, written 1958-68 and published abroad 1973-78, is The _________ Archipelago.
explanation: The Gulag Archipelago combined memoir, oral history from hundreds of survivors, and analysis. Solzhenitsyn was expelled from the Soviet Union in 1974 after Western publication. Earlier, his One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1962) had been published during a brief Khrushchev-era thaw. His exposure of the Gulag was historic.

prompt: How did Anna Akhmatova preserve her Stalin-era poem-sequence Requiem (composed 1935-1940) when writing it down was too dangerous?
options: She memorised it; she didn't dare write it down for years
correctAnswer: She memorised it; she didn't dare write it down for years
explanation: Akhmatova's son was repeatedly imprisoned. Requiem was a sequence about the women waiting outside Leningrad prisons for news of their men. Osip Mandelstam similarly recited his 1933 anti-Stalin poem to friends; someone reported him; he was arrested, exiled, and died in a labor camp in 1938. His widow Nadezhda memorised his unwritten poems and preserved them through decades.

prompt: Match each post-Soviet writer to a contribution:

pairs.right: Postmodern, satirical, often surreal novels (Omon Ra, Generation P)
Even more extreme; mixes parody, dystopian fantasy, disturbing imagery
Documentary-style oral histories of late- and post-Soviet experience; Nobel 2015

explanation: Russian literature continues. The conditions of writing have changed; the moral seriousness Pushkin established remains. Whether Russian literature in the 21st century will produce another Tolstoy or Dostoevsky is unanswerable, but the tradition is still being written — even as renewed political pressure since 2022 has driven many writers into exile or silence.
